message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"c7b0f34c15150067b163b617d86c1807be97dded6340cd79c3d8a5f094d65690","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tx-class-c:lineage:84","source_registry_sha256":"73669019241a96617275447ad5e45b56c17a2d4bd395699448d85850cfc5bafb","units":[{"unit_id":"sec04-u01","module_id":"sec04-m01","objective_ids":["sec04-u01"],"title":{"text":"Yielding at intersections","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Right-of-way is given, never taken, because yielding prevents crashes even when another driver breaks the rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Clear rules about which road yields let drivers predict each other at intersections.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Eli drives a gravel road that ends at a paved two-lane highway with no signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Unpaved roads yield to paved ones, and the road ending at a T must stop for the through street.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]},"result":{"text":"Eli stops, waits for a clear gap in through traffic, and then enters the paved road.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking that if you have the right-of-way, you may take it no matter what the other driver does.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},"correction":{"text":"Right-of-way is always given, never taken; you still yield to avoid a crash even when others ignore the rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Give it, never take it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are turning left at a green light and a car is coming straight toward you. Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"The oncoming car going straight goes first.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03"]},"rationale":{"text":"A left-turning driver yields to straight-through oncoming vehicles. The T-ending and private-exit rules separately require stopping; obey any controlling signs or signals as well.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who goes first","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right-of-way is given.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Rules for each intersection.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson begins the right-of-way section. Right-of-way rules decide who goes first when two road users want the same space. Texas starts with a principle: right-of-way is always given and never taken. Then come the specific rules: obey signs and signals, know which kind of road yields to another, and know who yields at uncontrolled crossings, on left turns, at private driveways, and at the end of a T-intersection. Many crashes happen at intersections, so these rules carry real weight, and practice questions often describe a scene and ask who should go first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Given, never taken","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield even when others break rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Injury crash fines are steep.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"Serious injury doubles the band.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Right-of-way is always given and never taken. That means you yield even when another driver ignores the rules, because being right does not undo a crash. Texas backs this with fines. If failing to yield causes a crash with bodily injury, the fine runs from five hundred to two thousand dollars. If it causes serious bodily injury, the fine runs from one thousand to four thousand dollars. So the rule protects people and also carries a cost for drivers who push ahead. When in doubt about who should go, the safe choice is to yield and let the other driver pass.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Which road yields","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Obey signs and signals first.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Narrow roads yield to wider ones.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Unpaved roads yield to paved.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"At intersections with signs or signals, you obey them. Where there are none, road type helps decide. A one-lane or two-lane road yields to a divided road or a road with three or more lanes. An unpaved road yields to a paved one. At an uncontrolled crossing between similar roads, yield to the vehicle on your right, and go only when the right is clear or the vehicle is far away, while still checking to your left. These rules let both drivers know what to expect before they reach the intersection, so watch the road type as you approach.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Left turns, driveways, T-endings","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Left turns yield to oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Private exits stop before the sidewalk.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"T-endings stop for the through street.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some movements always yield. When you turn left, you yield to oncoming traffic going straight through. When you leave a private driveway or entrance, you stop before the sidewalk and yield to all vehicles and pedestrians. When your road ends at a T-intersection, you stop and yield to traffic on the through street. Notice the difference in what is required. A left turn yields, but it does not always require a full stop. A private exit and a T-ending require you to stop first, then yield, before moving into traffic or across the walkway.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Yield versus stop first","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Left turn: yield to straight traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},{"text":"T-ending: stop, then yield.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},{"text":"Private exit: stop before sidewalk.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two kinds of yielding. A left turn yields to straight-through oncoming traffic, but you may keep rolling if the way is clear. A T-ending and a private exit are stricter. At a T-ending, stop and yield to vehicles on the through street. At a private exit, stop before the sidewalk and yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians. Learners sometimes think every yield means a full stop, or that a driveway exit only needs a slowdown. When a question describes a car leaving a parking lot onto a street, think stop before the sidewalk. When it describes a left turn at a green light, think yield to oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03","sec04-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the left turn","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Green light, turning left.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"A car comes straight at you.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are turning left at a green light, and a car is coming straight toward you from the other direction. Who goes first? Work out your answer before reading on. The oncoming car going straight goes first. Left turns yield to straight-through oncoming traffic, so you wait for a safe gap. You do not need a full stop if the way is clear, but you must not turn into the oncoming car's path. If you were instead pulling out of a private driveway, you would stop before the sidewalk and yield to everyone first.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Intersections in brief","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right-of-way is given, never taken.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Narrow and unpaved roads yield.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},{"text":"Left turns yield; T-endings stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Right-of-way is always given, never taken, and failure-to-yield crashes bring fines of five hundred to two thousand dollars for bodily injury and one thousand to four thousand for serious bodily injury. Obey signs and signals. One-lane and two-lane roads yield to divided or wider roads, and unpaved roads yield to paved ones. At uncontrolled crossings, yield to the right and still check left. Left turns yield to oncoming straight traffic, while private exits and T-endings stop first. Next, frontage roads and railroad crossings.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-R02","sec04-F03","sec04-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u02","module_id":"sec04-m02","objective_ids":["sec04-u02"],"title":{"text":"Frontage roads and rail crossings","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Trains always have priority at crossings, so drivers stop at the set distance from the rails and wait until it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Reporting broken crossing signals quickly helps keep other drivers safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Zoe's car stalls on the tracks and she hears a train horn.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Stalled drivers leave the car and run trackside toward the train.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},"result":{"text":"Zoe gets out and runs beside the tracks toward the train, away from where the car will be hit.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you may drive on once a train passes, even if the crossing lights are still flashing.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05"]},"correction":{"text":"At flashing red, hold until the train passes and the lights stop; at lowered gates, hold until the train passes and the gates rise.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop fifteen to fifty feet back.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Crossing gates are down and the train has just cleared. What do you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},"answer":{"text":"Keep waiting until the gates rise.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05"]},"rationale":{"text":"Lowered gates mean hold until the train passes and the gates go up; never go around them.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Frontage roads and trains","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Who yields on frontage roads.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"How to cross the tracks safely.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers two places where the right-of-way rules are especially strict. The first is frontage roads, the roads that run alongside highways, where drivers must yield to traffic entering and leaving the highway. The second is railroad crossings. Trains always have the right-of-way, and the handbook gives detailed rules about when to stop, where to stop, how long to wait, and what to do if your car stalls on the tracks. We will finish with how to report a crossing signal that is not working, so the problem can be fixed before it hurts someone.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Frontage roads and merging lanes","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Frontage drivers yield to highway traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Right entries yield to left entries.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Stop for rail warnings or trains.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a frontage road, you yield to vehicles entering or leaving the highway. When two lanes of traffic going the same direction merge, the entry from the right yields to the entry from the left. At railroad crossings, you must stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest rail when there are signals, gates, a flagger, or other warning devices, when a train is within about one thousand five hundred feet, when you hear a train's warning, or when a train is close and visible. Those are the triggers that require a full stop before the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"At the crossing","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay stopped until safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},{"text":"Never stop on the rails.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},{"text":"Open windows to hear whistles.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Once stopped at a crossing, you stay stopped until it is safe, or face a fine of fifty to two hundred dollars. At a crossbuck, look and listen with care. Hold through flashing red lights until the train passes and the lights stop. Hold at lowered gates until the train passes and the gates rise. Make sure there is room to clear every track before you cross, and never stop on the rails. Trains always have priority. Lower your windows and turn down the radio near crossings so you can hear a whistle in time to stop. Patience at a crossing is always the safer choice.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stalls and broken signals","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Push the car or get out.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Run trackside toward the train.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Report signals with the crossing number.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"If your car stalls on the tracks, push it off if you can, or get out and run beside the tracks toward the train. That is the direction the handbook gives, so learn it before you ever need it. If a crossing signal is not working, report it to DPS communications or local officers and give the crossing's ID number. In an emergency, use the railroad number on the blue-and-white notification sign at the crossing, along with the national crossing inventory number and a short description of the problem. Have the crossing number ready when you call it in.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Lights versus gates","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Flashing red: wait for lights to stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Lowered gates: wait for gates to rise.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Stalled: run toward the train.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two warnings that look similar. At flashing red lights, you wait until the train passes and the lights stop flashing. At lowered gates, you wait until the train passes and the gates rise. In both cases, the train passing is not enough on its own. The third piece of the trap is direction. If your car stalls, run beside the tracks toward the train, not away from it. When a question asks when you may cross, look for the lights going dark or the gates going up. Never race a train or drive around a lowered gate.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lowered gates","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Gates down, train just passed.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},{"text":"When may you go?","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: the crossing gates are down, and the train has just cleared the crossing. What do you do now? Work out your answer before reading on. You keep waiting until the gates rise. Lowered gates mean you hold until the train passes and the gates go up, and you never go around them. When they rise, make sure there is room to clear every track before you move, so you will not end up stopped on the rails. If the crossing had flashing red lights instead of gates, you would wait for the lights to stop. Patience here keeps you safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-R05","sec04-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Rail safety in brief","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Frontage drivers yield to highway traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Stop fifteen to fifty feet back.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Wait for lights off, gates up.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us wrap up. On frontage roads, yield to vehicles entering or leaving the highway, and merging entries from the right yield to entries from the left. Stop fifteen to fifty feet from the nearest rail for signals, gates, flaggers, warnings, or trains within about one thousand five hundred feet. Stay stopped until safe, wait for flashing lights to stop or gates to rise, never stop on the rails, and run trackside toward the train if stalled. Report a broken signal with the crossing's number. Next, emergency vehicles and school buses.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04","sec04-R04","sec04-F05","sec04-R05","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u03","module_id":"sec04-m03","objective_ids":["sec04-u03"],"title":{"text":"Emergency vehicles and school buses","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Emergency vehicles need a clear road to reach people in danger quickly.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Stopping for school buses protects children getting on and off.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"On a four-lane highway, Ben sees a stopped ambulance on the shoulder with its lights flashing.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Past a lit stopped emergency vehicle, drivers leave the nearest lane on multi-lane highways or slow down sharply.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"result":{"text":"Ben moves out of the lane next to the ambulance, or slows to twenty below the limit if he cannot change lanes.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you only stop for a school bus if you are traveling behind it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09"]},"correction":{"text":"When a school bus shows alternating red lights, traffic in both directions stops, except on a different road or at a protected loading zone.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Red lights flash, both ways stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A fire truck with siren on is behind you on a city street. What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]},"answer":{"text":"Pull to the right edge and stop, or slow and clear a path.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"Moving emergency vehicles get a right-edge stop or a slowed clear path, while stopped ones get a lane change or a sharp slowdown.","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Making way for others","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Emergency vehicles on a call.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-F09"]},{"text":"School buses loading children.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers two kinds of vehicles that always get special treatment on the road. Emergency vehicles using sirens, bells, or red lights need a clear path, and stopped emergency vehicles with lights on need extra room. School buses with flashing red lights stop traffic so children can get on and off safely. The rules differ depending on whether an emergency vehicle is moving or stopped, and school buses have a few exceptions. The penalties for ignoring a school bus are among the heaviest in the handbook, so we will cover them as well.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Moving emergency vehicles","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull to the right edge and stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Or slow and clear a path.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Follow no closer than five hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"When an emergency vehicle approaches using a siren, a bell, or red lights, give it the road. If traffic allows, pull to the right edge and stop; if unable to pull right, slow down and clear a path for it. If you are following a fire truck or an ambulance on an emergency run with lights on, stay at least five hundred feet behind. Do not drive, park, or block the area around a place where emergency crews are answering an alarm. These rules give emergency vehicles the road while moving and room to work when they arrive. Check your mirrors often so you notice an emergency vehicle early.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stopped emergency vehicles","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leave the nearest lane on multi-lane roads.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Or slow twenty below the limit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},{"text":"Five miles per hour on slow roads.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"When you pass a stopped emergency vehicle with its lights on, you must either move over or slow down. On a highway with more than one lane going your direction, leave the lane nearest the vehicle. If you cannot, slow to twenty miles per hour below the posted limit when that limit is twenty-five or more. Where the limit is under twenty-five, slow to less than five miles per hour. An officer on scene may direct you otherwise, and then you follow the officer. This rule gives room to the people working beside the road at a scene.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"School bus stops","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alternating red lights stop both directions.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]},{"text":"Wait for motion, a wave, or dark lights.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]},{"text":"Penalties climb with repeats and injuries.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"When a school bus shows alternating red lights, traffic in both directions stops. You stay stopped until the bus moves again, the bus driver waves you through, or the lights turn off. The exceptions are when the bus is on a different road or in a controlled-access loading zone without a pedestrian crossing. A first failure to stop brings a fine of five hundred to one thousand two hundred fifty dollars. A repeat within five years raises it to one thousand to two thousand dollars and may suspend your license for six months. Injury crashes bring jail.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Moving versus stopped","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Moving with siren: right edge, stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Stopped with lights: move over or slow.","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Different scenes, different rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two emergency rules. For an approaching emergency vehicle, stop at the right edge if traffic permits; otherwise slow and clear its path. Keep five hundred feet behind a fire truck answering an alarm or an ambulance flashing red lights. A stopped emergency vehicle with lights on gets something different: you move out of the nearest lane on a highway with at least two lanes in your direction or slow down sharply. Learners sometimes pull over and stop for a vehicle already parked at a scene, or only slow for one racing toward them. Ask first whether the emergency vehicle is moving or stopped.","fact_ids":["sec04-R06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the fire truck","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Siren behind you.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-R06","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are driving on a city street, and a fire truck with its siren on comes up behind you. What should you do? Work out your answer before reading on. If traffic permits, stop at the right edge; otherwise slow down and clear its path. Once it passes, if you end up following it, stay at least five hundred feet behind.
